prompt: Where is type inference never applied in a function declaration?
hint: Callers the compiler has not seen yet.

choices.text: Parameters
choices.why: Right: every parameter has its type written.

choices.text: The return type of a single-expression body
choices.why: That one can be inferred from the expression, as `isLong` showed.

choices.text: `val`s declared inside the body
choices.why: Inside the body, names are inferred exactly as in `main`.

choices.text: Default values of parameters, which need their own type
choices.why: A default takes the parameter's type; it does not carry a type of its own.

prompt: Inside `fun total(minutes: List<Int>): Int`, a line says `minutes = listOf()`. What happens?
hint: What kind of name is a parameter?

choices.text: It replaces the caller's list as well
choices.why: Even where it compiled, it would rebind a local name; here it does not compile at all.

choices.text: It works, and only this call sees an empty list
choices.why: That would be true of a `var`; a parameter is not one.

choices.text: It does not compile: a parameter is a `val`
choices.why: Right: make a local `var` if you need one, as `sum` is.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning about shadowing
choices.why: Shadowing is declaring a new name; assigning to a parameter is refused.

prompt: `fun hours(minutes: Int): Int` returns `minutes / 60` inside `if (minutes > 0)` and nothing else. Where does the compiler point?
hint: `Hours.kt:6:1`.

choices.text: At the `if`, asking for an `else`
choices.why: This `if` is a statement, so it needs no `else`; the function's end is what lacks a `return`.

choices.text: At the closing brace, with `missing return statement`
choices.why: Right: the path where `minutes` is zero or less ends there with nothing.

choices.text: At the call in `main`, since 90 is positive
choices.why: The compiler checks the function once, for every possible argument.

choices.text: Nowhere: it returns 0 by default
choices.why: Kotlin never makes up a return value.

prompt: A function declared at the top of a file, outside any class, is called a ___-level function.
hint: Where it lives in the file.

prompt: `fun isLong(minutes: Int) = minutes >= 60`. What is the cost of leaving its return type out?
hint: What decides the type, and what happens when that changes?

choices.text: It is checked only at run time
choices.why: The type is inferred and checked at compile time like any other.

choices.text: It returns `Any`, so callers must cast
choices.why: It returns `Boolean`, inferred from `>=`.

choices.text: Java callers cannot call a function whose type was inferred
choices.why: The compiled method has a concrete return type; Java sees it like any other.

choices.text: Editing the body changes the type for every caller
choices.why: Right: write the type on a function other code depends on.

prompt: Why is `fun label(minutes: Int) = if (minutes >= 60) "long"` refused?
hint: What is the value when the condition is false?

choices.text: A single-expression body cannot hold an `if`
choices.why: `label` with an `else` is exactly that, and it compiles.

choices.text: An `if` used as a value needs its `else`
choices.why: Right: without one there is no value for the false case.

choices.text: The return type must be written when there is an `if`
choices.why: The type is inferred fine once both branches exist.

choices.text: String literals need a `return` in front of them
choices.why: An expression body has no `return` at all.

prompt: Kotlin has no ternary operator, because `___` with an `else` is already an expression.
hint: `label` used it.

prompt: `describe(course, minutes = 30, done = false, date = "2026-11-02")`. How do you set only `done` to `true`?
hint: Positions cannot skip a parameter.

choices.text: `describe("Kotlin", true)`
choices.why: The second position is `minutes`, an `Int`, so `true` does not fit.

choices.text: `describe("Kotlin", , true)`
choices.why: An empty slot is not Kotlin syntax.

choices.text: `describe("Kotlin", done = true)`
choices.why: Right: the name skips `minutes` and leaves it at 30.

choices.text: Write an overload `describeDone(course)`
choices.why: That is the Java way the defaults replace.

prompt: `describe("Kotlin", done = true)` printed a line. How many minutes did it show?
hint: The default of the parameter that was skipped.

prompt: Which argument does section 04 say to name first, as a matter of habit?
hint: A reader cannot guess what it means.

choices.text: The first argument
choices.why: The first is the one a reader most often knows from the function's name.

choices.text: A `Boolean`
choices.why: Right: `done = true` says what `true` alone does not.

choices.text: Every `String`, so that the order stays free
choices.why: A course name passed first reads perfectly well without a name.

choices.text: Any argument longer than ten characters
choices.why: Length is not what makes a value obscure.

prompt: A Java class calls a Kotlin function that has two default parameters. Without any annotation, what does Java see?
hint: The JVM has no default arguments.

choices.text: Three overloads, one for each number of arguments
choices.why: That is what `@JvmOverloads` asks for; without it there is one.

choices.text: The defaults, applied automatically when Java leaves arguments out
choices.why: Java cannot leave arguments out; there is nothing to apply them to.

choices.text: One method that takes every parameter
choices.why: Right: Java must pass them all unless the function carries `@JvmOverloads`.

choices.text: Nothing; functions with defaults are invisible to Java
choices.why: They are visible, with every parameter required.

prompt: `week` is `intArrayOf(20, 25)`. What does `total(10, *week, 5)` return?
hint: The spread puts both elements in the middle.

prompt: Inside `fun total(vararg minutes: Int)`, what is the type of `minutes`?
hint: An array of plain `int` values on the JVM.

choices.text: `List<Int>`
choices.why: A `vararg` is an array, not a list.

choices.text: `Array<Int>`
choices.why: That would box every number; `Int` gets the primitive array.

choices.text: `IntArray`
choices.why: Right: cheaper than a list of boxed `Integer`s.

choices.text: `Int`, called once per value
choices.why: The function runs once, with every value gathered into one array.

prompt: What does `*` mean in `total(*week)`?
hint: It is not arithmetic.

choices.text: Pass the array's elements as separate arguments
choices.why: Right: it unpacks the array into the argument list.

choices.text: Pass a pointer to the array instead of a copy
choices.why: Kotlin has no pointers; `*` here only unpacks.

choices.text: Multiply each element by the next argument
choices.why: There is no multiplication; the result was a plain sum.

choices.text: Make the array mutable inside the function
choices.why: Mutability is not what `*` is about.

prompt: `fun log(vararg lines: String, prefix: String = "> ")`. What does `log("planned", "done", "* ")` print?
hint: Nothing marks where the lines stop.

choices.text: Two lines starting with `* `
choices.why: Only `prefix = "* "` would do that.

choices.text: Three lines starting with `> `, the last one being `> * `
choices.why: Right: the third string is one more line, and the prefix keeps its default.

choices.text: A compile error, as the third argument is ambiguous
choices.why: It is not ambiguous to the compiler: positional values after a `vararg` all join it.

choices.text: Two lines, and `* ` is ignored
choices.why: Kotlin ignores no argument.

prompt: In `Report.kt`, the local function `line` uses `course`. Where does `course` come from?
hint: Nobody passed it.

choices.text: It is a parameter of `line`
choices.why: `line` takes `label` and `value` only.

choices.text: From a top-level `val` of the same file
choices.why: There is none; it is `report`'s parameter.

choices.text: From the function that declares `line`
choices.why: Right: a local function reads its enclosing function's parameters and `val`s.

choices.text: `main` passes it implicitly, through the call to `report`
choices.why: `main` passes it to `report`; `line` reads it from `report`.

prompt: `private fun format(…)` sits at the top of `Planner.kt`. Who can call it?
hint: `Main.kt` tried.

choices.text: Any file compiled with it
choices.why: That is the default without `private`.

choices.text: Only code in `Planner.kt`
choices.why: Right: the compiler refused the call from `Main.kt` by name.

choices.text: Only `main`
choices.why: `main` lives in `Main.kt`, which was refused.

choices.text: Only functions declared below it in the file
choices.why: Order in the file does not matter to Kotlin.

prompt: `val result = log("planned 45 min")`, where `log` has a block body and no return type. What does `println(result)` print?
hint: `Unit` is a real value.

choices.text: `null`
choices.why: `log` returns `Unit`, which is not `null`.

choices.text: Nothing; it does not compile
choices.why: Storing a `Unit` is allowed.

choices.text: `kotlin.Unit`
choices.why: Right: the name of the one value of `Unit`.

choices.text: `void`
choices.why: Kotlin has no `void`; `Unit` plays its part.

prompt: Why does `input.toIntOrNull() ?: fail("…")` compile as an `Int`, when `fail` returns `Nothing`?
hint: Nothing has no values at all.

choices.text: Because `Nothing` is converted to `0` by the elvis operator
choices.why: There is no value to convert: `fail` never returns.

choices.text: Because `fail` is inlined into the expression
choices.why: Inlining has nothing to do with the type check.

choices.text: Because `Nothing` and `Int` are the same type on the JVM
choices.why: They are different types; `Nothing` fits under every type.

choices.text: Because `Nothing` fits any type
choices.why: Right: with no values, it can never be the wrong type.

prompt: Match each function to what it gives back.
hint: Two have no value; the others are what they say.

prompt: `report(load(), format(now()))` is called. Put the steps in the order they happen.
hint: Arguments first, left to right; an argument's own arguments before it.

prompt: `fun plan(course: String, minutes: Int = 30, done: Boolean = false)`. Which calls compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: Named arguments may be out of order; a positional one must still sit in its own place.

choices.text: `plan("Kotlin")`
choices.why: Yes: both defaults apply.

choices.text: `plan(done = true, course = "Kotlin")`
choices.why: Yes: all named, any order.

choices.text: `plan(minutes = 45, "Kotlin")`
choices.why: No: the positional `"Kotlin"` is out of its place, as in `Mixed.kt`.

choices.text: `plan("Kotlin", true)`
choices.why: No: the second position is `minutes`, an `Int`.
